column2: Dhrishtadyumna, Satyaki, the sons of Draupadi, Vrikodara, Janamejaya, Shikhandin and the heroic Prabhadrakas,
the Chedis, Kekayas, Panchalas, the twins and the Matsyas, armoured, rushed at Radheya, strikers wishing to slay him.
They showered him with weapons of many kinds and streams of arrows, crushing him, like clouds in the rains on a mountain.
Karna's sons, strikers wishing to save their father, and others of yours, O king, heroes, held back the heroes.
Sushena cut Bhimasena's bow with a broad-headed arrow, pierced Bhima in the chest with seven iron arrows, and roared.
Then Vrikodara, of terrible prowess, taking another very strong bow and stringing it, cut Sushena's bow.
Enraged, as if dancing, he pierced him with nine arrows and quickly pierced Karna with seventy-three sharp arrows.
And he felled Karna's son Satyasena, with horses, charioteer, banner and weapon, with ten arrows, in the sight of his friends.
His head, with face like the moon, struck off by a razor-arrow, looked beautiful, like a lotus fallen from its stalk.
Having slain Karna's son, Bhima again tormented your men; cutting the bows of Kripa and Hardikya, he tormented them also.
Piercing Duhshasana with three, Shakuni with six iron arrows, he made Uluka and Patri both chariotless.
Saying "Sushena, you are slain!", he took an arrow; Karna cut it and struck him with three.
Then Bhima took another well-jointed, keen arrow and loosed it at Sushena; Vrisha (Karna) cut that too.
Again Karna, wishing to save his son, pierced Bhimasena with seventy-three chariot-arrows, cruelly, with cruel arrows, wishing to kill him.
Sushena, taking an excellent bow able to bear a burden, tormented Nakula in arms and chest with five arrows.
Nakula, piercing him with twenty firm burden-bearing arrows, roared a mighty roar, striking fear into Karna.
O great king, Sushena, piercing him with ten swift arrows, quickly cut his bow with a razor-arrow, the great chariot-warrior.
Then, taking another bow, Nakula, overcome with rage, held Sushena back in battle with many arrows.
Covering the quarters with arrows, O king, that slayer of heroes struck his charioteer and then Sushena with three, and cut his very strong bow into three pieces with three broad-headed arrows.
Then, taking another bow, Sushena, overcome with rage, pierced Nakula with sixty and Sahadeva with seven.
That battle became very great and dreadful, like that of gods and asuras, as they quickly struck each other with arrows, each seeking the other's death.

Satyaki, having killed Vrishasena's charioteer with three arrows, cut his bow with a broad-headed one, killed his horses with seven, tore down his banner with one, and struck him in the heart with three.
Then, sunk down on his chariot but rising again after a moment, wishing to kill Shaineya, he came on with sword and shield.
As Vrishasena sprang forward, Satyaki quickly pierced sword and shield with ten boar-eared arrows.
Duhshasana, seeing him chariotless and weaponless, quickly placed him on his own chariot and carried him to another chariot.
Then, mounting another chariot, the great chariot-warrior Vrishasena, unassailable in battle, again guarded Karna's rear.
Shaineya, having made Duhshasana's chariot and horses charioteerless with nine fresh swift arrows, struck him in the forehead with three.
He, mounting another duly equipped chariot, fought again with the Pandavas, increasing Karna's strength.
Then Dhrishtadyumna pierced Karna with ten arrows, the sons of Draupadi with seventy-three, and Yuyudhana with seven.
Bhimasena with sixty-four, Sahadeva with five, Nakula with thirty arrows, Shatanika with seven, the hero Shikhandin with ten, and the king of dharma with a hundred.
These and other heroes, O king of kings, eager for victory, tormented the mighty-bowed charioteer's son in the great battle.
The charioteer's son, hero, tamer of foes, moving gracefully on his chariot, pierced each of them in return with ten sharp arrows.
There we saw Karna's power with weapons and the dexterity of the great soul, O great king; it was wondrous.
They did not see him taking arrows or aiming them, but only saw that great chariot-warrior loosing them in fury.
Heaven, sky, earth and quarters were suddenly filled with sharp arrows; the sky in that region appeared as if covered with red cloud.
Radheya, as if dancing, mighty, bow in hand, pierced each in return with three times as many arrows as had struck him.
Having pierced them again with ten each, he roared; with their horses, charioteers, banners and parasols gone, they gave way.
Crushing those mighty archers with showers of arrows, Radheya, scorcher of foes, entered the king's unobstructed divisions.
Having killed three hundred chariots of the never-retreating Chedis, Radheya then attacked Yudhishthira with sharp arrows.
Then the Pandavas, O king, and Shikhandin with Satyaki, protecting the king from Radheya, surrounded him.
Likewise all your mighty archers, striving, protected Karna, hard to resist in battle, on every side.
The sounds of instruments of many kinds arose, O lord of men, and the lion-roars of the never-retreating heroes.
Then the Kurus and Pandavas met again fearlessly—the Parthas led by Yudhishthira, we led by the charioteer's son.
Vrisha (Karna), cutting with hundreds of fierce arrows the thousands of weapons of many kinds sent by the foe, pierced them calmly.
He cut off their heads, arms and thighs on every side; slain, they fell to the earth, and others, broken, fled.
The Dravidas, Andhras and Nishadas, urged by Satyaki, again tormented Karna in battle, foot-soldiers wishing to kill him.
Without arms, heads or helmets, struck by Karna's arrows, they fell to the earth at once, like a sala forest cut down together.
Thus hundreds, thousands and tens of thousands of warriors in battle, slain, came to the earth with their bodies and filled the quarters with fame.
Then the Pandavas and Panchalas hemmed in Karna Vaikartana, enraged in battle like Death, as one restrains a disease with spells and herbs.
Crushing them, he again attacked Yudhishthira, like a violent disease beyond the reach of spells and herbs.
Hemmed in by the Pandavas, Panchalas and Kekayas, eager for the king, he could not pass beyond them, as death cannot pass a knower of Brahman.

Karna, Karna, vainly regarded, charioteer's son, hear my word: you always compete in battle with the glorious Phalguna and always trouble us, abiding by the counsel of Dhritarashtra's son.
mahabharata:8:33.12	Whatever your strength and valour, and your hatred of the Pandavas, show all of it today, taking up great manliness; I shall rid you today of your zeal for battle in the great fight.
Having said this, O great king, the son of Pandu pierced Karna with ten sharp iron arrows with golden feathers.
The charioteer's son, tamer of foes, the mighty archer, pierced him in return with nine calf-tooth arrows, laughing as it were, O Bharata.
Then the hero killed the two Panchala wheel-guards of the great soul (Yudhishthira) with two razor-arrows in the battle, with straight-jointed arrows.
Those two heroes at the king of dharma's sides shone near his chariot like the Vasus beside the moon.
Yudhishthira again pierced Karna with thirty arrows, struck Sushena and Satyasena with three each,
pierced Shalya with ninety and the charioteer's son with seventy-three, and their protectors with three straight arrows each.
Then Adhiratha's son, laughing and shaking his bow, split the king with a broad-headed arrow, pierced him with sixty and roared with joy.
Then the Pandava heroes rushed at Yudhishthira, wishing to save him from the charioteer's son, and tormented Karna with arrows.
Satyaki, Chekitana, Yuyutsu, the Pandya, Dhrishtadyumna, Shikhandin, the sons of Draupadi and the Prabhadrakas,
the twins, Bhimasena, the son of Shishupala, the Karushas, the remaining Matsyas, the Kekayas, the Kashis and Kosalas—these swift heroes held back Vasushena (Karna).
Janamejaya the Panchala pierced Karna with arrows—boar-eared arrows, iron arrows, nalikas, sharp shafts, calf-tooth arrows, vipathas, razor-edged arrows and sparrow-faced arrows.
With fierce weapons of many kinds, chariot-men, elephant-men, horsemen and foot-soldiers rushed on every side at Karna, surrounding him, wishing to kill him.
Attacked on all sides by the foremost of the Pandavas, he brought forth the Brahma weapon, filling the quarters with arrows.
Karna, a fire of great flames of arrows and heat of valour, ranged beautifully in battle, burning the Pandava forest.
Warding off the great weapons of the great souls, the mighty archer, laughing, cut the bow of the lord of men with arrows.
Then, aiming ninety straight-jointed arrows in a moment, Karna in battle split the king's armour with sharp arrows.
That golden armour, falling, shone like a lightning-bearing cloud, the remnant of the sun struck by the wind.
That body of the lord of men, its armour fallen, shone, adorned with jewels, like the sky at night.
Without armour, drenched in blood from the arrows, Partha, enraged, hurled an all-iron dart at Adhiratha's son.
As it blazed in the sky, the mighty archer cut it with seven arrows, and cut, it fell to the ground.
Then Yudhishthira struck Karna in the arms, forehead and heart with four javelins and roared with delight.
Karna, blood gushing, enraged, sighing like a serpent, cut his banner with a broad-headed arrow, pierced the Pandava with three, cut his quiver and shattered his chariot to bits.
Thus Partha withdrew, his rear-guard slain and his charioteer dead, unable to stand before Karna, despondent.
Pursuing him, Radheya touched his shoulder with his hand and said, laughing, O king, as if reproaching the Pandava:

How can one born in a noble family, fixed in the duty of a kshatriya, abandon his foes in battle and protect his life in the great fight?
mahabharata:8:33.38	I think you are not skilled in kshatriya duties; you are suited to the Brahmanic strength, to study and sacrificial work.
mahabharata:8:33.39	Do not fight me, son of Kunti, and do not approach heroes; do not speak ill of them, and do not go into the great battle.
Having said this, the mighty one released Partha and struck the Pandava army like the thunderbolt-wielder the asura host; then the king hurried away, as if ashamed.
As the king went, Achyuta, the Chedis, Pandavas and Panchalas followed him, with Satyaki the great chariot-warrior, the brave sons of Draupadi and the twin Pandavas.
Then, seeing Yudhishthira's army turn away, Karna with the Kuru heroes followed at their rear.
Then the Dhritarashtras' lion-roar arose with the sound of conches, kettledrums and bows.
Yudhishthira, O Kaurava, quickly mounting a chariot, saw Karna's prowess against Shrutakirti.
Seeing his army being driven, the king of dharma Yudhishthira, enraged, said to those warriors, "Kill him by thousands."
Then, permitted by the king, all the great chariot-warriors of the Pandavas led by Bhimasena ran at the sons.
A tumultuous sound arose of the warriors there, O Bharata, of elephants, horses, chariots, foot-soldiers and weapons here and there.
Rise! Strike! Advance! Attack!—saying so to one another, the warriors struck each other in the battlefield.
There was shade as of clouds in the sky by showers of arrows, with the best of men closing in and striking each other.
Without pennants, banners and parasols, with horses, charioteers and weapons lost, limbs and members scattered, they fell exhausted to the earth, their lords slain.
Like peaks of the foremost mountains, the best elephants with their riders fell slain, like mountains shattered by lightning.
With armour, ornaments and bodies cut, split and overturned, horses with their riders fell by thousands, their heroes slain.
Foot-soldiers by thousands, with weapons and limbs thrown about, were killed by elephants, horses, chariots and enemy heroes in the crush.
The earth was strewn on every side with the heads of warriors keen for battle, with wide long reddish eyes and faces like lotus and moon.
Then people heard in the wide sky the sound of songs and instruments from the celestial cars and hosts of apsarases.
Hosts of apsarases, taking up by thousands the heroes slain and cut, facing the enemy, carried them to the celestial cars.
Seeing that great marvel before their eyes, the heroes, glad at heart, desiring heaven, quickly rushed at each other.
Chariot-warriors fought wonderfully with chariot-warriors in battle, foot-soldiers with foot-soldiers, elephants with elephants, horses with horses.
While the battle thus went on, with destruction of elephants, horses and men, and the army covered with dust, they killed their own and the enemy alike.
The fight became hair-to-hair, tooth-to-tooth for elephants, nail-to-nail, fist-fight and wrestling, destroying the sin of the body.
As the battle went on with destruction of elephants, horses and men, rivers of blood flowed from the bodies of men, horses and elephants, and bore along many fallen bodies of them.
In the crush of men, horses and elephants, a blood-filled, most dreadful river, with a mire of blood, bore the bodies of men, horses and elephants, frightening the timid.
Those eager for victory crossed to its farther shore, some wading, others swimming, sinking and rising.
They, with limbs smeared with blood and their armour, weapons and clothing red, bathed in it, drank the blood and grew faint, O best of the Bharatas.
Chariots, horses, men, elephants, weapons, ornaments, garments, armour, those being slain and the slain—we saw earth, sky, heaven and the quarters nearly all red.
By the smell, touch and taste of the blood, by its excessive colour and by the spreading sound, a very great dejection came over most of the army, O Bharata.
That shattered army of yours was assailed again by the heroes led by Bhimasena, the chariot-warriors led by Satyaki.
Unable to bear the onslaught of those great souls, your sons' great army, O king, turned away.
With chariots, horses and elephants scattered, and men and horses in confusion, shields and armour shattered, weapons and bows thrown aside,
your army fled, tossed about on every side, like a herd of elephants harassed by lions in a great forest.
Then from flank, counter-flank and the south the Kurus, with weapons raised, rushed at Bhima in the battle.
Karna too, seeing Dhritarashtra's sons fleeing with faces turned away, sent his swan-white best horses to where Vrikodara was.
Sent by Shalya, ornament of the battle, O great king, the horses, reaching Bhimasena's chariot, clashed with it.
Seeing Karna approaching, Bhima, filled with rage, set his mind on Karna's destruction, O best of the Bharatas.
He said to the hero Satyaki and to Dhrishtadyumna, the Parshata: "Protect this king, the righteous Yudhishthira, who was somehow rescued from great peril and left before my eyes,
deprived of all his equipment in my presence for Duryodhana's sake by the evil Radheya.
Today, Parshata, I shall put an end to that sorrow; either I shall slay Karna in battle or he will slay me in the dreadful battle; this I tell you truly.
Today I entrust to you the king as a deposit; strive all of you, free of anxiety, to guard him."
Seeing Bhima coming swiftly, delighting in battle, the mighty lord of the Madras spoke to the charioteer's son:

See, Karna, the mighty-armed Pandava, enraged, surely wishing to discharge on you a rage cherished for a long time.
mahabharata:8:34.13	I have never before seen such a form of his—not when Abhimanyu was slain, nor when Karna, or the rakshasa Ghatotkacha was slain.
mahabharata:8:34.14	Capable of restraining the whole three worlds when enraged, he bears such a form, auspicious, like the fire of the end of time.
As the lord of the Madras spoke so to Radheya, O king, Vrikodara, blazing with anger, advanced on Karna.
Seeing Bhima come so, delighting in battle, Radheya, laughing as it were, spoke to Shalya:

What you have said to me today, lord of the Madras, regarding Bhimasena is true, no doubt.
mahabharata:8:34.18	This Vrikodara is brave, heroic, wrathful, indifferent to his body and life, and superior in strength.
mahabharata:8:34.19	While living incognito in Virata's city, out of desire to please Draupadi, relying on his arms only, hiding his nature, he slew Kichaka with his following.
mahabharata:8:34.20	Today, at the head of the battle, armed, overcome with rage, with a raised rod like a servant, he may go to battle even with Death.
mahabharata:8:34.21	This wish of mine is long cherished: to slay Arjuna in battle or be slain by Dhananjaya. Perhaps today it will be fulfilled through meeting Bhima.
mahabharata:8:34.22	If Bhima lies slain or made chariotless, then Partha will come against me, and that will be well for me. Quickly consider what you think proper here.
Hearing these words of the great-souled Radheya, Shalya said to the charioteer's son thus come:

You are advancing on mighty Bhimasena, mighty-armed one; having dispelled Bhimasena, you will then reach Phalguna.
mahabharata:8:34.25	The wish you have cherished in your heart for so long will surely be fulfilled, Karna; I tell you this truly.
Thus addressed, Karna said to Shalya again, "I shall slay Arjuna in battle or Dhananjaya will slay me. With mind fixed on battle, go, go!" and he urged him on.
Then Shalya quickly drove the chariot there, O lord of men, where mighty-bowed Bhima was routing the army.
Then the sound of trumpets and the great roar of kettledrums arose, O king of kings, at the meeting of Karna and Bhima.
Then Bhimasena, enraged, the strong one, routed your formidable army in all directions with spotless sharp iron arrows.
That clash, tumultuous, terrible, fierce, O lord of men, took place between Karna and the Pandava in the battle; then in a moment, O king of kings, the Pandava rushed at Karna.
Seeing him come, Karna Vaikartana, enraged, struck him in the chest with an iron arrow and covered him again with showers of arrows, the immeasurable one.
Pierced by the charioteer's son, he covered him with arrows and pierced Karna with nine straight-jointed sharp arrows.
Karna cut his bow in the middle in two with an arrow, and then pierced the bowless one in the chest with a very sharp iron arrow that pierces all armour.
Vrikodara, taking another bow, pierced the charioteer's son, O king, in his vital parts with very sharp arrows, knowing vitals, and roared a mighty roar, as if making heaven and earth tremble.
Karna tormented him with twenty-five iron arrows, as a proud rutting elephant in the forest is tormented by firebrands.
Then the Pandava, his limbs pierced by arrows, overcome with rage, his eyes red with fury and indignation, wishing to slay the charioteer's son,
fixed on his bow a mighty arrow of great speed, able to bear a burden, capable of splitting even mountains.
Drawing the strong bow back to his ear, that great archer, the wind's son, in anger loosed it, wishing to kill Karna.
That arrow, loosed by the strong one, with the sound of thunder, pierced Karna in battle like a thunderbolt a mountain.
Struck by Bhimasena, the charioteer's son, bearer of the Kuru burden, commander of the army, sank down senseless on the seat of his chariot.
Then the lord of the Madras, seeing the charioteer's son senseless, carried Karna, ornament of battle, away from the fight in the chariot.
When Karna was thus defeated, Bhimasena routed the great army of Dhritarashtra's sons, as Indra the army of the danavas.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "'Karna alone in battle can slay the Srinjayas with the Pandavas,' so Duryodhana told me again and again, charioteer.
Seeing Radheya defeated by Bhima in the encounter, what did my son Duryodhana then do?"
[Sanjaya said:] Seeing Radheya, the charioteer's son, bewildered in the great battle, O king, he spoke to his brothers with a great army:
Go quickly, good luck to you; protect Radheya, who is sinking in the sea of calamity, unfathomable with fear of Bhimasena.
Commanded by the king, wishing to kill Bhimasena, they advanced enraged, like moths into a fire.
Shrutayus, Durdhara, Karatha, Vivitsu, Vikata, Sama, Nishangin, Kavachin, Pashin, and Nanda and Upananda,
Dushpradharsha, Subahu, Vatavega and Suvarchas, Dhanurgraha, Durmada and Satvasama, Saha,
these valiant, mighty ones, surrounded by chariots, reached Bhimasena and encircled him on every side; they loosed flights of arrows with many marks in all directions.
Bhimasena, mighty, tormented by them, quickly killed, as those sons of yours attacked, fifty chariots with fifty chariots, O king.
Then, enraged, he struck off Vivitsu's head, with its earrings and helmet and like the full moon, with a broad-headed arrow, and he fell slain to the ground by Bhima, O great king.
Seeing that hero slain, his brothers rushed from every side in the battle at Bhima of terrible prowess.
Then with two other broad-headed arrows Bhima, of terrible prowess, took the lives of two of your sons in the great battle.
They fell to earth like two trees struck by the wind, Vikata and Sama, like two sons of gods, O king.
Then Bhima swiftly sent Kratha to Yama's abode with a very sharp iron arrow; he fell slain to the earth.
Then a terrible cry of "Alas!" arose, O lord of men, as your sons, bowmen, were being slain.
While their army was in disorder, mighty Bhimasena sent Nanda and Upananda to Yama's abode in the battle.
Then your sons fled in fear, overcome, seeing Bhimasena in battle like Death the ender.
Seeing your sons slain, the great-minded charioteer's son again sent his swan-white horses to where the Pandava was.
Sent by the king of the Madras, O great king, the horses, swift, reached Bhimasena's chariot and clashed with it.
Entering the city swiftly, raising his arms, grieved and trembling, he entered the king's house.
When my son Duryodhana was slain by unrighteous means, dear one, what did Kritavarman, Kripa and Drona's son do, Sanjaya?
And hearing of Duryodhana, like a roaring bull, the slaying of Duhshasana, Karna's reversal, and the eclipse of the sun that was Drona, my heart is torn.
What will the Vrishni's daughter-in-law, my son's wife, say to Madhusudana Krishna, Hari, when he goes back from here to Dvaraka?
[Gautami said:] "Release him, you without understanding; Arjunaka, he is not to be killed by you. Who, thinking, would take on a burden when what is to be obtained is certain?"
Consecrate King Yudhishthira, the righteous; he will protect this earth by dharma, self-controlled.
On pleasure excursions the Kuru king Yudhishthira, of great splendour, would grant all desires to Ambika's son.
Thus addressed, they, deceived and affronted, replied; hear, lord of men, what the sages said to them.
Then, having honoured the townsfolk and country people, the righteous king set his mind on departure, and his brothers too.
And whatever other afflictions befell you through the dice or in battles or elsewhere, you ought not to remember them.
